# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

There is a common belief, woven deep into how most organizations operate, that a successful meeting is one where everyone leaves nodding. The room reaches agreement, heads bob, someone volunteers to write up the "action items," and people file out satisfied. Harmony, we assume, is the sign that things went well.

But this belief deserves scrutiny. Agreement is not always what it appears to be. Sometimes it reflects genuine shared understanding. Just as often, it conceals confusion, unspoken doubt, or the quiet exhaustion of people who simply want the meeting to end. A room full of nodding heads can be a room full of people who are each picturing something slightly different, or who privately believe the plan will fail but don't want to be the one to say so.

The alternative is counterintuitive: a genuinely productive meeting can end not with agreement but with a precise, honest map of what people disagree about. Instead of papering over differences, the group names them. Instead of forcing a premature decision, the group identifies exactly what evidence would settle the question and who will go gather it. Disagreement, in this framing, is not a failure of the meeting.
